stem:
A woman at eight weeks is reviewed by an early-pregnancy registrar for vaginal spotting. Ultrasound shows a viable intrauterine pregnancy with a closed cervix. She has had two previous confirmed first-trimester miscarriages; investigation did not identify antiphospholipid syndrome. She is stable and asks whether a medicine can improve this pregnancy’s chance of continuing.

Which treatment is most appropriate to offer?

options.label: A
options.explanation: Aspirin is used for other indications, including selected pre-eclampsia prevention and antiphospholipid-related pregnancy care; it is not the indicated treatment for this presentation.

options.label: B
options.explanation: There is no identified thrombotic or antiphospholipid indication for heparin, and empirical anticoagulation is not the recommended response to this bleeding pattern.

options.label: C
options.text: Vaginal micronised progesterone until the bleeding stops
options.explanation: For this eligible patient with a confirmed heartbeat, the recommended progesterone course continues to 16 weeks; cessation of spotting is not the specified stopping point.

options.label: D
options.explanation: Current bleeding with two previous losses meets Australian progesterone eligibility, and the heartbeat supports continuation to 16 weeks. The recommended preparation is vaginal micronised progesterone, usually 400 mg twice daily.

options.label: E
options.text: Intramuscular hCG injections during the first trimester
options.explanation: hCG injections are not the recommended evidence-based intervention for threatened miscarriage in this setting.

context: Current early-pregnancy bleeding plus previous miscarriages can justify vaginal micronised progesterone after confirming an intrauterine pregnancy.
